chunks.section: Abstract
chunks.text: Spectral variants of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) choose both a subspace and which factor to freeze. We separate these choices by freezing the input factor A A or output factor B B on the top or bottom singular directions of pretrained weights, with learning rates selected separately. At rank 2, the same-band advantage of freezing A A is larger than either within-factor band difference on all four task–model pairs with complete comparisons. Freezing B B also trails comparable-budget free LoRA by 8–18 percentage points on five pairs spanning a formatting task and OpenBookQA. The A-frozen advantage persists in a single-GPU-model replication and within individual MLP module groups, including controls with equal or greater trainable counts for B frozen, and when A is frozen on a random orthonormal basis. The factor contrast weakens with rank. On OpenBookQA / Qwen2.5-1.5B at rank 16, PEFT’s MiCA implementation trails comparable-budget LoRA by 3.08 points under a shared training recipe transferred from the MiCA paper. A trained oracle output subspace largely removes the low-rank deficit; partial warm-up gains recur across three direction seeds. The factor-versus-band ordering is descriptive; an approximate multiplicity audit weakens several earlier significance claims. These results extend known factor asymmetry by showing how its magnitude depends on spectral placement, rank and training conditions.

chunks.section: 1 Introduction
chunks.text: LoRA adapts a pretrained weight matrix through a low-rank update B ​ A BA , where A A maps the layer input into a small intermediate representation and B B maps that representation to the output ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Fixing one factor reduces the number of trainable parameters, but also fixes either the input or output subspace available to the update. A spectral construction makes another choice: which singular directions of the pretrained weight should define that subspace? Cross-method comparisons can entangle these choices. MiCA fixes the output factor on bottom singular directions ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) ; PiCa’s implementation fixes an input-side projector on top directions and shares the trainable output factor across layers ( Hwang et al., 2026 ) . These correspond to freezing B B and A A , respectively (Appendix C.3 ). Comparing them changes orientation, band and sharing at once. Their within-method band ablations, by contrast, hold orientation fixed. The asymmetry between LoRA factors is already known. Zhu et al. (2024) show that training B B while fixing A A is often more effective than the reverse, including experiments with spectral factors. LoRA-FA fixes A A for memory efficiency ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and LoRA+ improves training by assigning a larger learning rate to B B ( Hayou et al., 2024a ) . The question we address is narrower: how large is the frozen-factor contrast relative to the top-versus-bottom spectral contrast, and how does that comparison change with rank?

chunks.section: 1 Introduction
chunks.text: We use a two-by-two design: freeze A A or B B , each on the top or bottom band, while retaining the same pretrained model, data, adapted modules and training budget. Learning rates are selected separately for every configuration. We complement equal-rank comparisons with free LoRA at a nearby trainable-parameter count and a control that gives the B-frozen configuration more parameters than the A-frozen configuration. Figure 1 illustrates the main low-rank result. Figure 1: At rank 2, changing the frozen factor has a larger effect than switching spectral extremes. Points are mean test scores over five seeds at separately selected learning rates. The free-LoRA reference has rank 1 and a comparable, slightly larger trainable budget than rank-2 B-frozen LoRA. A-frozen LoRA has more trainable parameters at equal rank; Table 3 controls this advantage. The panels use different vertical scales. Lines connect configurations, not training trajectories. Full scores and uncertainty are in Tables 7 and 2 . At rank 2, the factor contrast exceeds the band contrast on all four complete comparisons. The A-frozen advantage survives parameter-count and module-group controls and does not require a spectral input basis on the two pairs tested. The factor contrast decreases along the complete OpenBookQA rank sweep, becoming comparable to the band contrast at rank 16. Finally, a subspace extracted from trained LoRA greatly improves B-frozen performance, showing that its low-rank deficit depends on placement.

chunks.section: 1 Introduction
chunks.text: Our contribution is to separate these design choices under optimization and budget controls and identify the limits of the resulting comparison. Factor asymmetry itself is not new. A follow-up evaluates PEFT’s MiCA implementation under a transferred recipe, without reproducing its original knowledge-acquisition benchmark or evaluating PiCa.

chunks.section: 2.2 Equal rank and comparable budget answer different questions
chunks.text: An equal-rank comparison holds the maximum matrix rank fixed, but generally gives A-frozen and B-frozen adapters different parameter counts. Summed over all adapted modules, A-frozen adapters at the same rank contain 15.0% more parameters on Llama-3.2-1B and 26.8% more on Qwen2.5-1.5B. This follows from the models’ input and output widths, not from an additional learned component. For a second comparison, we select an integer rank k k for free LoRA that gives a nearby trainable budget. At frozen rank 2, the reference has rank 1: its count exceeds the B-frozen count by 7.5% on Llama-3.2-1B and 13.4% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. At frozen rank 16, Qwen uses a rank-7 reference, within about 2.5% of the B-frozen count on the two Qwen sizes. Appendix C gives the counts. We call this a comparable-budget reference , rather than an exact budget match. It changes both the accessible update space and rank, so its gap cannot identify the isolated causal effect of freezing a factor. Reference choice matters: on Format / Llama-3.2-1B, equal-rank free LoRA scores 80.33% over five seeds with 2.15 times the B-frozen count (supplementary record, Table S14). The top-band deficit is then 15.90 points, versus 12.41 against the rank-1 reference. To test whether parameter count alone explains the A-frozen advantage, we also compare A frozen at rank 2 against B frozen at rank 3. This gives B frozen the larger count on two models. We do not infer memory, wall-clock or total-compute equivalence from trainable counts.

chunks.section: 2.3 Tasks, models and optimization
chunks.text: The central rank-2 results cover five task–model pairs: a synthetic formatting task on Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B, and OpenBookQA on Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3. Both frozen orientations are evaluated on four pairs; the formatting experiment on Qwen2.5-1.5B has no A-frozen arm. ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge provide additional benchmark checks. The complete A/B rank sweep covers ranks 2, 4, 8 and 16 on OpenBookQA with Qwen2.5-1.5B, with rank-16 checks on other pairs. Rank-32 results on ARC-Challenge concern B-frozen configurations only. The formatting task transforms CoNLL-2003 sentences into an invented structured output ( Tjong Kim Sang and De Meulder, 2003 ) . Its transformations include rewriting person names, sorting lists, spelling out an entity count and constructing an entity-initial signature. A strict verifier scores whether every required rule is satisfied on 614 test items. This is a measure of learning a structured output transformation, not a general reasoning benchmark. OpenBookQA and ARC use multiple-choice accuracy ( Mihaylov et al., 2018 ; Clark et al., 2018 ) . Each answer option is scored by mean conditional log-likelihood per token; the highest-scoring option is selected. OpenBookQA uses 500 test questions.

chunks.section: 2.3 Tasks, models and optimization
chunks.text: Unless stated otherwise, experiments adapt the query, key, value and output projections and the MLP gate, up and down projections in every transformer layer. The standard budget is 600,000 supervised tokens, with AdamW, zero weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.0 and a cosine schedule. The effective batch is 32 sequences of at most 384 tokens. Formatting loss covers the target only; the default OpenBookQA and ARC loss covers packed question–answer text. An answer-only control is reported separately. Identical token budgets imply different numbers of steps and epochs across tasks (Appendix D ). Learning rates are selected independently for each configuration on validation scores, normally using seeds 0 and 1, and test results are then reported on seeds 2–6. Rates span 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 10 − 2 10^{-2} in the main grid, with extensions when a maximum occurs at an edge. The formatting replication on Qwen uses reporting seeds 22–26. New module-group controls use eight reporting seeds, 2–9, and the MiCA follow-up uses a shared transferred recipe rather than separately tuned rates. Selection exceptions, residual grid-boundary cases and hardware differences are documented in Appendix D.3 . Separate tuning reduces a known evaluation bias ( Lee et al., 2026 ) ; it does not establish that every optimizer configuration has reached its global optimum.

chunks.text: Many campaign comparisons were specified in internal version-control records before their corresponding runs, after earlier experiments had already informed the research program. We call these prespecified campaign comparisons , not externally preregistered tests. The supplementary record dates these protocols and lists every historical test with its status. An approximate post hoc Holm audit of 145 historical test rows retains 46 of the 109 previously positive decisions. chunks.text: Against comparable-budget free LoRA, the top- and bottom-band B-frozen configurations lose 8–18 points on the five central pairs (Table 7 ). chunks.text: The preceding count control still combines modules with different shapes. We therefore repeat the comparison while adapting only the MLP down projections, or only its gate and up projections, on Format / Llama-3.2-1B and OpenBookQA / Qwen2.5-1.5B. All runs use RTX 4000 Ada GPUs, separately selected learning rates and eight reporting seeds. Within down projections, freezing A A at rank 2 gives fewer trainable parameters than freezing B B at rank 2, yet scores higher on both bands. Neither total count nor allocation across module types therefore explains the ordering, though geometry can affect its magnitude. chunks.section: 3.3 Training controls and remaining optimization effects
chunks.text: Three controls test narrower alternatives. On Llama’s formatting task, quadrupling the supervised-token budget and retuning every learning rate reduces the cost of fixing B B , but leaves equal-rank deficits of 12.0 and 18.2 points relative to training both factors. A fresh five-seed replication also retains the large gap; its factor contrast is 15.21 points versus an absolute band contrast of 2.96 points. On OpenBookQA with Qwen2.5-1.5B, supervising answers only preserves A-frozen advantages of 7.2 and 9.7 points. This last control holds the number of optimizer steps and the packed sequences fixed, while reducing supervised tokens by about sixfold; it tests loss masking rather than an equal-supervision training regime. Appendix E gives the measurements. Making both factors trainable from the same spectral initialization also restores most of the performance, including at the comparable-budget rank. Once B B is trainable, however, it can leave the initial band. The disappearance of a band difference in this control is therefore expected and is not independent evidence that the original band was irrelevant. The data also leave room for optimization effects. On the formatting task, fixed singular-value scaling improves the top-band B-frozen score by 3.61 points, and a fixed scalar per module improves it by 2.31 points without changing the accessible subspace. The scalar is determined from the pretrained spectrum; it is not an extra learned parameter. Loss curves continue to decrease at the original training endpoint. These observations prevent interpreting the remaining gap as a measured approximation-error floor.

chunks.section: 3.3 Training controls and remaining optimization effects
chunks.text: A separate replication reruns all seven central formatting configurations on RTX 4000 Ada at their original selected rates. The A-frozen advantages are 13.16 and 19.67 points (top and bottom), and the free-LoRA gaps are 12.74 and 18.66 points. All retain their campaign decisions. This removes differences in GPU model as an explanation for this replication, while leaving the historical scores unchanged (Appendix E.1 ).

chunks.section: 4.1 MiCA under a transferred training recipe
chunks.text: Does the rank-16 bottom-band deficit depend on our training recipe? We evaluate PEFT 0.21.0’s MiCA implementation on OpenBookQA / Qwen2.5-1.5B, transferring the learning rate and four-epoch schedule of MiCA’s rank-16 BLOGS configuration ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) . We retain our data, 384-token packing, scoring rule and seven adapted module types. This tests MiCA in our setting, rather than reproducing the original benchmark. MiCA reaches 52.40%, 2.56 points above our bottom-band arm, but trails a fresh comparable-budget free-LoRA run by 3.72 points (Table 6 ). That comparison changes both recipe and training amount. After observing it, we specify and run a second test with free LoRA under the same transferred recipe as MiCA. Free LoRA still leads by 3.08 points, with a nominal paired- t t 95% interval of [ 1.34 , 4.82 ] [1.34,4.82] . The two methods then use the same 417,792 supervised tokens and 272 optimizer steps; free LoRA has 0.79% fewer trainable parameters. This follow-up supports a deficit under one shared recipe. It does not establish the best attainable performance of either method or reproduce MiCA’s acquisition–retention comparison. Appendix C.4 gives the settings and the adaptive sequence of tests. chunks.section: 5 Can a frozen output subspace support good adaptation?
chunks.text: The preceding comparisons could suggest that fixing B B is inherently ineffective. A simple oracle experiment tests that interpretation. We first train a free LoRA at rank 2 on the same training data. For each module, we extract an orthonormal basis Q Q of its learned output-factor space, freeze a new adapter’s B B on Q Q , and train its A A from zero. This is an oracle with respect to access to a trained subspace , not access to test labels. The reason this is a useful diagnostic is algebraic. If the trained teacher has factors B ∗ , A ∗ B^{*},A^{*} and B ∗ = Q ​ M B^{*}=QM , then B ∗ ​ A ∗ = Q ⁡ ( M ​ A ∗ ) . B^{*}A^{*}=Q(MA^{*}). (4) Thus the teacher’s update is representable with B = Q B=Q fixed. This identity is not a new capacity theorem. The empirical question is whether retraining the remaining factor from zero finds a useful solution, and how informative the result is about cheaper choices of Q Q . On OpenBookQA with Qwen2.5-1.5B, oracle directions from two independently trained teachers yield 55.88% and 55.28% accuracy, compared with 46.52% for the top-band B-frozen configuration and 54.84% for a free rank-1 reference retrained in the diagnostic campaign. On Llama’s formatting task, one teacher basis gives 80.81%, close to the five-seed free-LoRA mean of 80.33% at rank 2. These results show that a fixed output basis can support high performance in the tested settings. They do not prove that optimization difficulty is absent for arbitrary bases.

chunks.section: 5.1 Which placements are available before training?
chunks.text: We compare the spectral extremes with an independently drawn random orthonormal output basis and the top two left singular vectors of the gradient of the training loss with respect to W 0 W_{0} . The gradient is estimated either from 64 training sequences or from the entire training set. All resulting adapters keep B B fixed and train A A ; they do not implement LoRA-GA, LoRA-One or LoRA-SB. Neither random nor initial-gradient placement removes the observed deficit (Table 19 ). Accumulating the gradient over all training sequences does not improve this conclusion on OpenBookQA. On the formatting task, its gain over the top spectral band is 1.79 points, with a nominal 95% interval of [ − 0.84 , 4.42 ] [-0.84,4.42] . This excludes the large recovery seen with the oracle in this experiment, but should not be read as a statement about all gradient-derived subspaces, ranks or optimizers. Figure 3: Training-derived output directions are more useful in these diagnostics. Gains relative to top-band B frozen, at rank 2, with nominal paired- t t 95% intervals over five retraining seeds. Dashed lines mark the earlier free-LoRA gaps used as fixed campaign reference values: 8.04 and 12.41 points. Teacher-subspace uncertainty is not included. On the formatting task, the 64-sequence gradient and oracle use a retrained top-band reference, whereas the full-gradient and warm-up comparisons use the original reference; the two reference scores differ by 0.13 points. Full details are in Appendix F .

chunks.section: 5.2 How early do useful directions emerge?
chunks.text: A short warm-up of a free rank-2 LoRA provides an intermediate diagnostic. After a chosen fraction of training steps, we freeze its output basis and retrain A A from zero over the remaining steps. The total number of steps is unchanged, but both factors train during warm-up. The original direction seed and two new seeds give the same qualitative pattern: longer warm-up produces larger mean gains at the tested 5%, 10% and 25% cuts (Figure 4 ). At 10%, gains over top-band B frozen span 4.12–4.64 points on OpenBookQA and 6.09–7.79 points on the formatting task. Each of the four new comparisons passes the Bonferroni correction for that family. Nevertheless, none of their corrected intervals establishes recovery of at least 70% of the fixed earlier free-LoRA gap. Appendix F.3 gives the conditional intervals and references. Figure 4: Warm-up gains recur across three direction seeds. Each point averages five retraining seeds for one learned output basis. Recovery is the gain over the original top-band B-frozen reference divided by its fixed free-LoRA gap (8.04 points on OpenBookQA; 12.41 on Format). Lines connect three tested cuts; they are not a fitted learning curve. The pattern is descriptive, and values above one can arise because the reference uses rank 1 while warm-up uses rank 2. Corrected intervals for the new 10% comparisons appear in Table 20 . The full oracle requires a separate rank-2 teacher run followed by adapter retraining. Warm-up keeps the step count fixed but changes which factors train during those steps. Neither is a demonstrated gain in total compute or memory efficiency. Both show that the choice of fixed output subspace can matter much more than the difference between the two spectral extremes.

chunks.section: Factor asymmetry and freezing.
chunks.text: Zhu et al. (2024) are the closest precedent: they compare the two frozen orientations, study orthonormal factors and report a top-spectral B-frozen result essentially equal to a random B-frozen result on GLUE at rank 16. LoRA-FA ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) and LoRA+ ( Hayou et al., 2024a ) also establish that the factors have distinct practical roles; initialization changes their optimization dynamics ( Hayou et al., 2024b ) . Kratsios et al. (2025) study generalization of asymmetric adapters with frozen random factors. We extend the empirical comparison to both spectral extremes, separately tuned rates, very low ranks and controls that reverse the parameter-count advantage. We do not treat tuning or frozen-factor asymmetry themselves as new contributions.

chunks.section: Pretrained spectral structure.
chunks.text: PiSSA and MiLoRA initialize trainable low-rank factors from different parts of the pretrained spectrum ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . MiCA keeps its output subspace fixed ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) ; PiCa uses a fixed input-side projector in its implementation together with parameter sharing ( Hwang et al., 2026 ) . LoRA-XS learns a small core within a spectral construction ( Bałazy et al., 2024 ) , while SVFT learns sparse coefficients between pretrained singular vectors ( Lingam et al., 2024 ) . Quercia et al. (2026) already show the value of intermediate components for performance–forgetting trade-offs in spectral initialization. Our interior-band observation is a secondary result about a frozen output subspace, not the discovery of intermediate spectral components. In speech adaptation, SSVD also keeps output-associated singular vectors fixed ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , underscoring the need to limit general claims about the cost of this constraint.

chunks.section: Data-dependent and changing subspaces.
chunks.text: LoRA-GA and LoRA-One use gradient information to initialize adapters whose factors remain trainable ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . LoRA-SB instead trains a small core between fixed factors obtained from an approximation to an initial update ( Ponkshe et al., 2024 ) . EVA and CorDA use activation or context information ( Paischer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . TLoRA constructs a task-aware input subspace from weights and input covariance, fixes A A , and trains B B with additional rank and scale allocation ( Lin et al., 2026 ) . These constructions differ from fixing only the leading left singular vectors of our initial-gradient estimate. GaLore refreshes gradient-projection subspaces during training ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) ; Flora interprets low-rank adapters as gradient compressors ( Hao et al., 2024 ) ; VeRA learns scaling vectors around shared random factors ( Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) . Our negative gradient diagnostic does not evaluate these complete methods. Recent work on factor-constrained continual learning likewise studies how factor constraints translate into effective updates, but targets historical-feature protection rather than our single-task top-versus-bottom comparison ( Wang et al., 2026 ) .

chunks.section: Evaluation and optimization.
chunks.text: Lee et al. (2026) show that separately tuning learning rates can remove apparent advantages of several LoRA variants. Our own selections illustrate the issue. On Format / Llama-3.2-1B at rank 2, bottom-band B frozen selects 5 ⋅ 10 − 3 5\cdot 10^{-3} , half the top band’s 10 − 2 10^{-2} (Table 14 ). It also selects a lower rate on OpenBookQA at ranks 4 and 8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B and rank 16 on Qwen2.5-7B. Historical common-rate comparisons can even reverse the ranking (Appendix D.3 ). Lee and Lee (2026) identify batch size as another important evaluation axis. Our low-rank B-frozen gaps survive the learning-rate search used here, but batch size remains fixed and not every training configuration is shown to converge. The conclusion concerns the reported training budgets and hyperparameters.

chunks.section: What the comparison identifies.
chunks.text: At rank 2, the factor contrast exceeds the top/bottom contrasts on all four complete pairs. This ordering does not extend to arbitrary subspace placement, as the oracle shows. Equal-rank and comparable-budget comparisons control different quantities. Count and module-group controls support the A-frozen advantage, but scalar rescaling and longer training show that optimization also contributes to the measured deficits.

chunks.section: Scope.
chunks.text: The strongest evidence concerns Format and OpenBookQA. The larger models are tested on OpenBookQA, Mistral only at rank 2; complete rank-4 and rank-8 comparisons cover one pair. ARC-Challenge shows different higher-rank behavior. We establish neither a universal rank threshold nor a ranking of complete MiCA and PiCa methods. The MiCA follow-up covers one model, task and transferred recipe, without assessing acquisition–forgetting trade-offs.

chunks.section: Uncertainty and selection.
chunks.text: Five reporting seeds give limited precision for small effects and ratios. Intervals condition on test items; a seed-and-item bootstrap widened selected Format intervals by 1.8–2.6 times. OpenBookQA lacks the retained predictions for that analysis. Corrections apply within campaigns; the approximate 145-row Holm audit reduces historical positive decisions and excludes the new experiments. The decomposition remains exploratory. Retrospective power calculations often require 3–5-point band differences for 80% detection probability; non-significance does not establish equivalence. Oracle and warm-up intervals condition on each learned basis, and random-basis variability is not isolated from retraining randomness. Rate selection on two seeds adds uncertainty absent from these intervals. The random-A replication was prespecified but not blind to earlier outcomes.

chunks.section: Hardware and reproducibility.
chunks.text: Of 137 historical score cells, 86 use RTX 4000 Ada only and 51 mix GPU models; six individual GPU records are missing. The seven-arm Format replication uses RTX 4000 Ada throughout, strengthening that result without balancing other historical campaigns. Protocol timestamps establish chronology within the repository, not external registration. Exact reproduction requires the original data-building, training and evaluation artifacts in addition to the aggregates.

chunks.section: 8 Conclusion
chunks.text: At rank 2, the frozen-factor contrast exceeds the contrast between spectral extremes. The A-frozen advantage survives count and module controls and, on two pairs, a random input basis. It weakens with rank and varies by task and model. Learned output bases greatly improve B-frozen performance. Across complete all-module comparisons at ranks 2–8, means favor A frozen on both bands; free LoRA scores higher or within 1.4 points. Comparisons should report orientation, basis construction and scale, tuned hyperparameters, trainable counts and subspace-learning cost.

chunks.text: For an orthonormal fixed Q ∈ ℝ d out × r Q\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} , { Q ​ A : A ∈ ℝ r × d in } = { Δ ​ W : col ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) ⊆ col ⁡ ( Q ) } . \{QA:A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\mathrm{in}}}\}=\{\Delta W:\operatorname{col}(\Delta W)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(Q)\}. For an input basis P ∈ ℝ d in × r P\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times r} with orthonormal columns, the analogous A-frozen set is { B ​ P ⊤ } \{BP^{\top}\} , whose row space lies in row ⁡ ( P ⊤ ) \operatorname{row}(P^{\top}) . Given a target update T T , its best Frobenius approximations in these spaces are Q ​ Q ⊤ ​ T QQ^{\top}T and T ​ P ​ P ⊤ TPP^{\top} . These projection identities explain the constraints but do not identify the target update preferred by a nonlinear network or the solution found by AdamW. A change of basis Q ↦ Q ​ O Q\mapsto QO with O O orthogonal leaves the reachable update set unchanged. It need not leave coordinate-wise AdamW dynamics unchanged. This distinction also applies to small within-band rotations caused by finite-precision SVD computations. Column-sign changes can be absorbed by matching row-sign changes in A A , but general rotations do not establish optimizer equivalence.

chunks.section: C.2 SVD precision and the bottom band
chunks.text: The complete thin SVD is computed in fp32; singular values are retained in fp32 and singular vectors are stored in fp16. With zero-based indices, a band at relative position β ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \beta\in[0,1] begins at ⌊ β ⁡ ( m − r ) ⌋ \lfloor\beta(m-r)\rfloor and includes the next r r directions. The main two bands use β = 0 \beta=0 and β = 1 \beta=1 . A random spectral-index baseline selects r r columns of U U without replacement; it is distinct from the random orthonormal baseline, which is independent of W 0 W_{0} . No numerical threshold removes small singular values in the reported runs. For a rectangular matrix, a thin SVD omits the additional structural null-space directions on the larger side. It may still contain zero or numerically near-zero singular values if the weight is rank deficient. Near-degenerate directions also make individual singular vectors less stable than their spanned subspace. An implementation check against PEFT 0.21.0’s MiCA initialization used a common fp32 SVD on 14 Qwen2.5-1.5B modules at rank 2 and found matching initialized factors, trainable parameters, outputs and gradients on A A . With the actual fp16 caches, checks across all 308 adapted modules of Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B at ranks 2 and 16 found a maximum principal-angle sine of 5.8 ⋅ 10 − 3 5.8\cdot 10^{-3} , with median values between 2 ⋅ 10 − 4 2\cdot 10^{-4} and 9 ⋅ 10 − 4 9\cdot 10^{-4} . These are numerical subspace checks, not end-to-end equivalence tests of the training recipes.

chunks.section: C.3 Relation to MiCA and PiCa
chunks.text: The B-frozen bottom configuration follows MiCA’s parameterization: the left singular vectors at the bottom of the pretrained weight’s thin SVD define fixed B B , and A A starts at zero. The scaling, adapted modules, tasks, training lengths and hyperparameter search follow our protocol. The controlled arm reproduces this construction. The separate PEFT follow-up in Section 4.1 transfers selected training settings from Rüdiger and Raschka (2026) , with the adaptations specified below. PiCa’s paper and PyTorch weight storage use transposed conventions. Its official LinearWithPiCa implementation computes the right singular vectors of a weight stored with shape ( d out , d in ) (d_{\mathrm{out}},d_{\mathrm{in}}) , registers the top r r rows as a fixed buffer P P , and trains M ∈ ℝ d out × r M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} . Its effective update is M ​ P MP . Consequently P P corresponds to our A A and M M to our B B . This can be inspected in pica/pica_layer.py of the official repository at revision 8fa738b70b0c03e7643515695f1e9e6785ec3778 . 1 1 1 https://github.com/hjunseoh/PiCa . The cited revision fixes the inspected implementation; it is not a revision of our experimental code. Its shared trainable factor is a further difference from our layer-specific adapters. PiCa’s Gemma-2B projection ablation is at rank 256, whereas our central A/B comparison is at rank 2. We did not execute PiCa and do not infer its relative benchmark performance from the present results.

chunks.section: C.4 PEFT MiCA follow-up: transferred settings
chunks.text: The PEFT arm uses init_lora_weights="mica" , r = α = 16 r=\alpha=16 , fixed B B and initially zero A A . We take learning rate 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 5\cdot 10^{-4} and four epochs from the MiCA paper’s rank-16 Llama-2-7B BLOGS entry, together with its cosine schedule, 10% warm-up, weight decay 0.01, adapter dropout 0.05, gradient clipping 0.3 and batch size four without accumulation. We use AdamW and retain our OpenBookQA loader, 384-token blocks, precision and evaluator. The original study uses a 512-token limit and normally adapts query and value projections; we retain all seven module types. Its base-to-instruct weight composition is not part of this benchmark protocol. Hence “transferred recipe” denotes these explicit settings, not a full replication. The first campaign trains MiCA and reruns our bottom B-frozen and free-LoRA references on seeds 2–6. It specifies one two-sided paired test of free LoRA minus MiCA at level 0.05 ( t > 2.776 t>2.776 , four degrees of freedom). MiCA minus our bottom arm is 2.56 ​ [ 1.30 , 3.82 ] 2.56\ [1.30,3.82] points, descriptively. The four-epoch and main recipes differ in both supervised tokens and optimizer steps (Table 6 ).

chunks.section: C.4 PEFT MiCA follow-up: transferred settings
chunks.text: The shared-recipe test was planned after this result. It uses PEFT’s standard initialization ( init_lora_weights=True ), r = α = 7 r=\alpha=7 , and the same data, modules and training settings as the MiCA arm. Its five new LoRA runs are paired with the existing five MiCA runs. The protocol fixes the same nominal 0.05 test before these new runs, but the comparison is an adaptively chosen follow-up, not an independent replication of MiCA. Free LoRA’s change from the main to the transferred recipe is − 0.64 ​ [ − 1.41 , 0.13 ] -0.64\ [-1.41,0.13] points; this interval does not establish equivalence. Neither method is independently retuned in the shared-recipe test, and the transferred rate need not favor either method on this task.

chunks.section: D.1 Training configuration
chunks.text: The backbones belong to the Llama, Qwen2.5 and Mistral families ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Qwen Team, 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) . The main configuration uses AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) with ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999) , zero weight decay, clipping at 1.0, bf16 model weights and gradient checkpointing. The cosine schedule uses a 5% warm-up. The effective batch is two sequences per micro-batch with 16 accumulation steps. Setting α = r \alpha=r maintains a scale of one across ranks. Free LoRA initializes A A using the Kaiming construction ( He et al., 2015 ) and B B at zero; neither spectral trainable control modifies W 0 W_{0} at initialization. The supervised-token counter is incremented at every forward pass, and training stops after the optimizer step that reaches the token budget. The accumulation counter spans epoch boundaries, with gradients cleared after each optimizer step. The standard runs require 274 steps (2.76 epochs) for the Llama formatting task, 49 steps (5.76 epochs) for OpenBookQA and 49 steps (14.93 epochs) for ARC-Challenge. Thus the 600,000-token budget is a nominal stopping target and can be exceeded by the final complete step. On OpenBookQA and ARC, training examples contain the question and the correct answer text, without distractor options. They are concatenated and packed into blocks of 384 tokens. Every token is supervised in the default setting. Evaluation uses the prompt “Question: … Answer:” and scores each candidate answer by score ⁡ ( a ∣ q ) = 1 | a | ​ ∑ t = 1 | a | log ⁡ p ⁡ ( a t ∣ q , a < t ) . \operatorname{score}(a\mid q)=\frac{1}{|a|}\sum_{t=1}^{|a|}\log p(a_{t}\mid q,a_{<t}).

chunks.section: D.1 Training configuration
chunks.text: The reported metric is the fraction of questions for which the highest-scoring candidate is correct. Training uses each benchmark’s own training split. Public benchmark scores do not constitute a guarantee against pretraining contamination.

chunks.section: D.2 Formatting task and verifier
chunks.text: Sentences are drawn from CoNLL-2003 and retained when they contain at least three entities. Targets require person names in last-name-first order, alphabetically sorted lists, an entity count written in words, and entity initials in document order. The verifier enforces tags, single-line JSON, the required keys and their order, and the target’s transformation rules. A generation passes only if all checks succeed. The task therefore combines entity handling, transformations and serialization; “valid-format accuracy” is stricter than merely syntactic JSON validity. The training set used by the full-gradient diagnostic contains 3,178 sequences. Evaluation generates at most 128 tokens on 614 test items. Across main rank-2 configurations, 0.7–0.9% of generations reach that limit. Component-level checks place the larger bottom-band deficits in the signature and entity-count fields rather than the presence of keys. Exact reproduction of this custom metric requires the data generator, prompt template, split manifest and verifier implementation, not merely the verbal description. Runs predating verifier-version logging were checked where possible. Saved generations from 91 runs were rescored and matched their recorded scores. Fifteen reported runs without saved generations were repeated and replaced. Five repetitions matched the original score exactly; the other ten moved by − 2.6 -2.6 to + 3.6 +3.6 points, with a mean change of + 0.1 +0.1 . This is consistent with run variability but does not by itself prove the absence of an earlier verifier difference.

chunks.section: D.3 Learning-rate search and its exceptions
chunks.text: The main initial grid is { 10 − 4 , 5 ⋅ 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 , 2 ⋅ 10 − 3 } \{10^{-4},5\cdot 10^{-4},10^{-3},2\cdot 10^{-3}\} , extended to 5 ⋅ 10 − 3 5\cdot 10^{-3} and 10 − 2 10^{-2} when needed. Position sweeps additionally use 2 ⋅ 10 − 2 2\cdot 10^{-2} . The rank-16 OpenBookQA search spans seven rates from 10 − 4 10^{-4} to 2 ⋅ 10 − 2 2\cdot 10^{-2} . Validation scores, normally averaged over seeds 0 and 1, select the rate. No test-set optimum replaces this selection in the main score tables. The main formatting selection uses a 400-item validation evaluation. The rank-2 bottom-band tie on Llama was additionally evaluated on selection seeds 30–32. The wider experimental record also contains two selections whose independence from reporting seeds was not established. The main rate-selection principle should therefore not be interpreted as a claim that every historical selection was strictly independent. The fresh-seed replication and the separately specified extension campaigns reduce reliance on these early choices without resolving them retrospectively. Some campaign grids end at a selected boundary: the rank-2 bottom B-frozen arm on Qwen2.5-7B and the top A-frozen arm on Mistral select the lowest tested rate. In the four-times-longer formatting control, top-initialized both-trainable LoRA selects the lowest rate and free LoRA the highest. These configurations retain their observed optima over the tested grids; an untested rate is not ruled out. The parameter-reversal and rank-extension campaigns have interior selected rates. In the answer-only campaign, the bottom A-frozen grid was extended to 2 ⋅ 10 − 2 2\cdot 10^{-2} , after which 10 − 2 10^{-2} remained the selected rate.

chunks.section: D.3 Learning-rate search and its exceptions
chunks.text: For the complete rank extensions on OpenBookQA, the selected rates for B-top, B-bottom, A-top, A-bottom and the free reference, in that order, are ( 5 , 2 , 5 , 2 , 5 ) ⋅ 10 − 3 (5,2,5,2,5)\cdot 10^{-3} at rank 4 on Qwen2.5-1.5B, ( 5 , 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 ) ⋅ 10 − 3 (5,1,2,2,2)\cdot 10^{-3} at rank 8 on that model, and ( 1 , 0.5 , 1 , 0.5 , 0.5 ) ⋅ 10 − 3 (1,0.5,1,0.5,0.5)\cdot 10^{-3} at rank 16 on Qwen2.5-7B. Frozen ranks and reference ranks are distinguished in Table 9 . A post hoc sensitivity analysis that chooses the best rate on reporting seeds is optimistic and is not a valid replacement for validation-based model selection. Several rank-16 auxiliary verdicts changed under that analysis, further motivating the descriptive treatment of small higher-rank effects.

chunks.section: Lower selected rates and curvature.
chunks.text: At rank 2 on the formatting task, the two-seed selections on Llama-3.2-1B and an additional model, Qwen2.5-0.5B, give bottom-band B frozen half the rate of the other B-frozen configurations ( 5 ⋅ 10 − 3 5\cdot 10^{-3} versus 10 − 2 10^{-2} ). A five-seed validation selection supports a lower bottom-band rate on four of five Llama seeds, but only partly on OpenBookQA. Its reading rules were recorded three minutes after launch, before results were read (supplementary record, §S16.2). Post hoc Llama curvature measurements estimate the largest eigenvalue λ max \lambda_{\max} of the training-loss Hessian H H restricted to each configuration’s trainable directions. The estimator uses power iteration on H + c ​ I H+cI , with the shift estimated in an unshifted pass, and retains the largest of five restarts. At initialization, the bottom-band median is 333, versus 29–33 for top, random-index and random orthonormal configurations. At step 274, bottom remains higher than top (23.33 versus 6.95). All 15 paired bottom-to-other ratios at initialization exceed two, while the product of λ max \lambda_{\max} and the selected learning rate η \eta is 5.1–5.7 times larger for bottom (supplementary record, §S23.3). This is consistent with the direction of the rate shift, but neither explains its magnitude nor establishes its cause. Lee et al. (2026) similarly relate method-specific optimal learning rates to the largest loss-Hessian eigenvalue across LoRA variants. The raw Hessian omits AdamW’s preconditioning, and the eigenvalue estimates have numerical uncertainty.

chunks.section: Rankings at a common learning rate.
chunks.text: Historical formatting experiments show reversals in the ranking by mean score on Llama-3.2-1B at ranks 2 and 4, and Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen2.5-1.5B at rank 2 (supplementary record, §S23.4). On Llama at rank 2, bottom leads the best other B-frozen mean by 2.15 points at 2 ⋅ 10 − 3 2\cdot 10^{-3} , but trails the best other mean by 14.43 points at 10 − 2 10^{-2} . These extrema use different competitors and need not equal the seed-paired contrasts. The bottom advantage paired over seeds 2–6 at the lower rate is only 0.98 points, with a nominal paired- t t 95% interval of [ − 1.4 , 3.4 ] [-1.4,3.4] , so this half of the reversal is not established. Both halves pass their original nominal paired- t t tests ( t > 2.776 t>2.776 , four degrees of freedom) only on Qwen2.5-0.5B, where one reused cell predates a protocol that described it as new. The Llama rank-2 analysis is post hoc, and the other three configurations have prespecified campaign protocols. These observations motivate separate rate selection without establishing a universal reversal across tasks or ranks.

chunks.section: F.1 Initial gradients and accumulated gradients
chunks.text: For each adapted module, the gradient of the training loss with respect to W 0 W_{0} is measured at the unadapted model. Its top two left singular vectors define fixed B B . The 64-sequence estimator uses sampling seed 1000. The accumulated estimator uses nested sets so that its first 64 sequences reproduce the original estimator; the full sets contain 272 packed sequences on OpenBookQA and 3,178 sequences on the formatting task. Gradients are accumulated per module in a separate process and reset after each micro-batch; no optimizer update is taken when constructing the basis. The construction records a double-precision SVD for this gradient diagnostic. The top-two share of gradient energy changes little as the sample increases: approximately 0.83 on OpenBookQA and 0.555–0.558 on the formatting task. Capturing much of the initial gradient energy therefore does not guarantee a useful fixed subspace throughout fine-tuning. It does not follow that the gradient is uninformative under a different rank, covariance metric or subspace-refresh rule. For the 64-sequence comparison, the top-band reference is 46.52% on OpenBookQA and a rerun score of 64.30% on the formatting task. chunks.section: F.2 Oracle and warm-up construction
chunks.text: The oracle teacher is a free rank-2 LoRA trained on the same training data. An orthonormal basis of its output-factor column space is used for a new rank-2 B-frozen adapter, with A A retrained from zero. OpenBookQA uses teacher seeds 0 and 7; the formatting task uses teacher seed 0. The first oracle campaign followed a declared launch decision after an earlier geometric diagnostic: the original trigger did not specify how to aggregate its seven module types, and its strict all-module interpretation was not met. Its stated comparison was retained. Consequently the oracle is presented as a follow-up diagnostic, without claiming an untouched preregistered discovery path. On OpenBookQA, the two teacher bases give gains over the original top reference of 9.36 [ 8.42 , 10.30 ] [8.42,10.30] and 8.76 [ 7.66 , 9.86 ] [7.66,9.86] points. chunks.section: G.2 Approximate multiplicity audit of the historical record
chunks.text: A post hoc audit applies Holm’s step-down calculation at 0.05 to 145 rows of the earlier campaign test inventory. The inventory starts from 151 rows, excludes four descriptive rows and two selection outcomes, and counts a row once even when it contains several quantities. This population is larger than the comparisons retained in this manuscript and excludes the new training campaigns. The 151 inventory rows are in Tables S24–S27 of the supplementary record. Removing the four descriptive rows and two selection outcomes gives the 145 audited rows. For reported t t statistics, the audit reconstructs p p -values using the recorded degrees of freedom and sidedness. For percentile-bootstrap intervals it instead estimates a standard error from the distance to the relevant endpoint divided by 1.96, then uses a normal tail. Other interval-based decisions are inverted using their stated thresholds. Rows without a statistical test receive p = 1 p=1 while remaining explicitly outside inferential interpretation. If a row originally declared several components positive, the largest of their p p -values is used; otherwise the smallest component value is used. One interval-based row also selects the smaller of two one-sided values. These data-dependent aggregation rules and approximate conversions prevent interpreting the output as rigorous error control over all underlying hypotheses.

chunks.section: G.4 Why recovery is not a causal decomposition
chunks.text: Earlier campaign summaries used G = L − b G=L-b , R = u − b R=u-b and I = L − u I=L-u , where L L is free LoRA at the reference rank, u u is a both-trainable spectral initialization at that rank, and b b is a B-frozen score at the larger frozen rank. The identity G = R + I G=R+I holds by construction. It does not establish that R R is a separately identified causal contribution of freezing, because moving from b b to u u also changes rank, parameterization and trainable count. The original recovery criterion asks whether a nominal interval for R R lies above 0.7 ​ G 0 0.7G_{0} , with G 0 G_{0} fixed from an earlier campaign and a two-point floor. This tests performance against a fixed numerical benchmark. It does not propagate uncertainty or covariance in an estimated G G , and is not a test of R − 0.7 ​ G R-0.7G under joint sampling. Its strongest interpretation is that spectral initialization need not prevent a trainable adapter from approaching the free reference. The paper therefore places direct A/B comparisons and the parameter-count reversal ahead of this statistic.

chunks.section: G.6 Hardware, retained artifacts and compute
chunks.text: Training uses a shared cluster with RTX 4000 Ada, RTX 2000 Ada, RTX A5000, RTX A4000 and GeForce RTX 3090 GPUs. The final audit identifies 137 distinct historical score cells, classifying 86 as RTX 4000 Ada only and 51 as mixed-GPU. It resolves 133 of 134 distinct recorded score values. Its per-run counts are 577 RTX 4000 Ada, 39 RTX 3090, 33 RTX 2000 Ada, 27 RTX A5000 and 23 RTX A4000, with six missing records: three each in the original rank-2 Format B-top and B-bottom cells. These counts sum to 705 records, of which 699 have a known GPU; 577/699 is 82.5%. Classification follows available metadata, and assignment is not balanced retrospectively. The unmatched score is the 59.05% formatting bottom control quoted in an earlier diagnostic caption. Parameter-reversal and rank-extension campaigns use RTX 4000 Ada throughout, as do the 681 follow-up runs preceding the random-A replication. The seven-arm formatting replication directly addresses the two central cells with missing records (Appendix E.1 ). Re-evaluation on the original GPU model reproduced the checked scores, whereas 11 of 12 re-evaluations on another GPU model differed; observed shifts were 0.2–1.8 points. This association is consistent with hardware-dependent numerical behavior, but does not isolate its exact kernel-level cause. Seed variation captures random hardware effects only to the extent that assignment varies appropriately; it cannot rule out systematic confounding.

chunks.section: G.6 Hardware, retained artifacts and compute
chunks.text: Runs failing an SVD reconstruction check were excluded before training. Two earlier runs on a subsequently suspect node were repeated elsewhere and replaced under a rule fixed before inspecting replacement scores. Memory failures caused by concurrent cluster use also led to relaunches. Factors were not retained for every extension run because of storage constraints, limiting retrospective geometric analyses. The recorded software stack is PyTorch 2.14.0 with CUDA 13.0, Transformers 5.17.0, Datasets 5.0.1, Safetensors 0.8.0 and NumPy 2.2.6. Nineteen of the original 1,242 runs predate a cluster upgrade and used PyTorch 2.5.1 with CUDA 12.1. Two belong to reported cells; rerunning them on the newer version changed their scores by − 0.16 -0.16 and + 0.65 +0.65 points. The exact association between versions and runs requires the per-run manifests.

chunks.section: G.6 Hardware, retained artifacts and compute
chunks.text: The reported accounting is 1,242 original runs (256 GPU-hours), 539 later runs (179 GPU-hours) and 838 extension runs (116.1 GPU-hours): 2,619 training runs and approximately 551 GPU-hours. This includes selection and follow-up work beyond the reduced set of comparisons emphasized in this manuscript. It excludes failed or superseded runs and substantial non-training work such as SVD caches, some gradient measurements and evaluation. The broader exploratory project reports 6,545 completed executions and 1,069 GPU-hours, using an execution-based count that is not directly interchangeable with the campaign count. The first follow-up campaigns add 681 runs and 61.3 GPU-hours: boundary selection 24/3.4, single GPU model 35/5.0, PEFT MiCA 15/0.8, shared recipe 5/0.2, module groups 538/45.9, and warm-up seeds 64/6.0 (runs/hours). The random-A replication adds 53 runs and 5.2 GPU-hours (36 selection, 2 extension, 15 reporting), bringing the campaign-based total to 3,353 training runs and approximately 617.6 GPU-hours. The post hoc audits launch no training runs. These totals include research and selection costs, not just the cost of any one adapter.

chunks.section: Reproducibility materials.
chunks.text: This manuscript includes the retained aggregate scores, configuration definitions, parameter formulas and interpretation rules. Code, protocols and run records are provided in the supplementary material, including the custom-task generator and verifier. Exact reproduction additionally depends on the model and dataset revisions and on the split and selection manifests. The run records allow the seed-level intervals to be recomputed, but the recorded campaign chronology cannot be verified independently of the private repository.
